1.title: Evaluating the Robustness
1.notes:
Good morning.

I'm Lello Molinario, and my thesis evaluates the operational robustness of AI-based forensic tools under adversarial and anti-forensic image manipulation.

2.title: How Do Manipulated Images Affect
2.notes:
AI can help forensic examiners decide which images to review first.

But what happens when an image is manipulated?

The relevant content may still be present, but the AI tool may fail to identify it.

This means that important images could be overlooked, while irrelevant images could receive unnecessary attention.

My research investigates how these errors occur and how they affect automated forensic triage.

3.title: Research problem and questions
3.notes:
Accuracy on clean images is not enough.

My research focuses on four questions.

First, how do AI systems behave with manipulated or out-of-distribution images?

Second, can adversarial attacks transfer between different models?

Third, how do commercial tools respond to attacks and different settings?

Finally, what are the forensic implications of false positives and false negatives?

4.title: From Prior Work to the Research Gap
4.notes:
Previous research has explored AI-assisted digital forensics, adversarial attacks, and anti-forensic manipulation.

In particular, Sanna and colleagues examined how forensic AI tools respond to manipulated images.

My thesis builds on these studies by introducing a traceable protocol to evaluate different systems, attacks, and classification errors within a common framework.

5.title: FAIRLab: A Traceable Evaluation Protocol
5.notes:
To study this problem, I designed and implemented FAIRLab.

It connects each original image to its modified versions, the settings used, and the results produced by each system.

Each source has a stable identifier and a recorded hash, so the evaluation can be traced back to the original file.

FAIRLab supports both white-box and black-box testing.

Its main contribution is a consistent and auditable evaluation process.

6.title: Dataset and Experimental Design
6.notes:
I started with almost twenty thousand candidate files from five collections.

After validation and duplicate removal, 15,321 unique images remained.

From these, one reviewer selected 1,500 images: 500 with weapons, 500 without weapons, and 500 outside the binary task.

The 1,000 weapon and non-weapon images formed the binary test set.

I evaluated them clean and under ten manipulation conditions: five adversarial or adversarial-style, and five anti-forensic.

In total, the evaluation bundle contained 11,500 files, including 500 clean out-of-distribution images.

The modified images remain linked to their original sources.

7.title: Evaluated Systems and Threat Model
7.notes:
For model-dependent attacks, I used EfficientNet-B0 as the white-box source model.

This means I could access its scores and gradients to generate the attacks.

I then tested whether the same images affected ResNet18 and a CLIP-based classifier.

Finally, I evaluated four families of commercial tools across six configurations, using only their observable outputs.

These experimental models are not replicas of the commercial systems.

The objective is to compare their responses under a defined threat model, not to declare an overall winner.

8.title: Attack Conditions and Evaluation Metrics
8.notes:
I tested ten manipulation conditions.

Four attacks targeted EfficientNet-B0: FGSM, Sigma Zero, One Pixel, and SuperDeepFool.

Color Shift was a model-agnostic condition.

The five anti-forensic transformations included JPEG recompression, resizing, blur, histogram modification, and contrast stretching.

For each condition, I compared the system output with its clean baseline.

I measured accuracy, missed weapon images, and false alerts.

Out-of-distribution results were evaluated separately, because they do not have binary ground-truth labels.

9.title: White-Box Results: Source Failure and Limited Transfer
9.notes:
The strongest result appears in the white-box source model.

EfficientNet-B0 achieved 97.8 percent accuracy on clean images, but only 1.5 percent under Sigma Zero.

However, the same attack did not cause a similar collapse in the receiving models.

ResNet18 remained at 96.8 percent, and CLIP at 94.4 percent.

This shows limited attack transfer in our tested setting.

It does not mean that these receiving models are generally resistant to adversarial attacks.

10.title: Commercial Black-Box Results: Selected Effects
10.notes:
Commercial tools showed different error patterns.

Under Sigma Zero, Excire D80 accuracy dropped from 91.5 to 65.7 percent. False alerts increased from 78 to 331.

Under FGSM, Magnet.AI missed 96 weapon images, compared with 35 on clean inputs.

An anti-forensic histogram modification also reduced Excire D80 accuracy by 3.7 percentage points.

These changes matter because missed relevant images and extra alerts have different implications for forensic triage.

Importantly, the attacks were generated against the source model, not directly against these commercial tools.

These are selected experimental effects, not a product ranking.

11.title: Out-of-Distribution Behavior
11.notes:
I also tested 500 images outside the weapon versus non-weapon task.

For example, CLIP assigned the weapon label to 83.6 percent of its out-of-distribution evaluations.

Among the commercial configurations shown here, the corresponding rates ranged from 26 to 36 percent.

These numbers describe how often a weapon label was produced.

They are not accuracy values, and they should not automatically be interpreted as false positives.

This is important because unexpected inputs may still receive a forensic classification label.

12.title: Conclusions and Future Work
12.notes:
The main conclusion is that high accuracy on clean images does not guarantee operational robustness.

The source model was highly vulnerable to some attacks, but the failures did not consistently transfer to other models.

Commercial outputs also depended on the attack and the configuration, while out-of-distribution inputs produced separate concerns.

FAIRLab provides a traceable way to study these effects, not a certification of commercial products.

Future work should include larger datasets, direct attacks against each model, and real analyst-centered evaluations.

AI should support forensic judgment, not replace it.
